claim: Non-canonical Wnt signaling plays a central role for coordinated cell polarization and directed migration in metazoan development.
source: Non-canonical Wnt signaling plays a central role for coordinated cell polarization and directed migration in metazoan development.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about Wnt signaling.

claim: Spatiotemporally restricted activation of non-canonical Wnt-signaling drives cell polarization in epithelial tissues.
source: While spatiotemporally restricted activation of non-canonical Wnt-signaling drives cell polarization in epithelial tissues, it remains unclear whether such instructive activity is also critical for directed mesenchymal cell migration.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about Wnt signaling in epithelial tissues.

claim: It remains unclear whether instructive activity of non-canonical Wnt signaling is critical for directed mesenchymal cell migration.
source: While spatiotemporally restricted activation of non-canonical Wnt-signaling drives cell polarization in epithelial tissues, it remains unclear whether such instructive activity is also critical for directed mesenchymal cell migration.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: A light-activated version of the non-canonical Wnt receptor Frizzled 7 (Fz7) was developed.
source: Here, we developed a light-activated version of the non-canonical Wnt receptor Frizzled 7 (Fz7) to analyze how restricted activation of non-canonical Wnt signaling affects directed anterior axial mesendoderm (prechordal plate, ppl) cell migration within the zebrafish gastrula.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the development of the Opto-Fz7 tool.

claim: Fz7 signaling is required for ppl cell protrusion formation and migration.
source: We found that Fz7 signaling is required for ppl cell protrusion formation and migration and that spatiotemporally restricted ectopic activation is capable of redirecting their migration.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Spatiotemporally restricted ectopic activation of Fz7 is capable of redirecting ppl cell migration.
source: We found that Fz7 signaling is required for ppl cell protrusion formation and migration and that spatiotemporally restricted ectopic activation is capable of redirecting their migration.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Uniform activation of Fz7 signaling in ppl cells fully rescues defective directed cell migration in fz7 mutant embryos.
source: Finally, we show that uniform activation of Fz7 signaling in ppl cells fully rescues defective directed cell migration in fz7 mutant embryos.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt signaling functions permissively rather than instructively in directed mesenchymal cell migration during gastrulation.
source: Together, our findings reveal that in contrast to the situation in epithelial cells, non-canonical Wnt signaling functions permissively rather than instructively in directed mesenchymal cell migration during gastrulation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the rescue experiments with uniform activation.

claim: Core components of the Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling module were initially identified in Drosophila to determine coordinated planar polarity of epithelial cells.
source: Initially, core components of the Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling module were identified in Drosophila to determine coordinated planar polarity of epithelial cells (Gubb and García-Bellido, 1982; Lawrence and Shelton, 1975; Vinson and Adler, 1987; Seifert and Mlodzik, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Vertebrate orthologs of key Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling components are required for both epithelial planar cell polarity and coordinated mesenchymal cell polarization, migration and intercalation.
source: Subsequently, vertebrate orthologs of key Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling components were shown to be required for both epithelial planar cell polarity and coordinated mesenchymal cell polarization, migration and intercalation (Gray et al., 2011; Singh and Mlodzik, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Signaling molecules and mechanisms determining epithelial cell polarity are largely conserved between vertebrate and invertebrate organisms.
source: Notably, signaling molecules and mechanisms determining epithelial cell polarity are largely conserved between vertebrate and invertebrate organisms indicating the general importance of Wnt-Fz/PCP in animal development (Yang and Mlodzik, 2015; Seifert and Mlodzik, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The key feature of Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling to achieve epithelial cell polarization is the polarized subcellular distribution of Wnt-Fz/PCP components in a tissue-wide and coordinated manner.
source: The key feature of Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling to achieve epithelial cell polarization is the polarized subcellular distribution of Wnt-Fz/PCP components in a tissue-wide and coordinated manner (Strutt, 2001; Feiguin et al., 2001; Tree et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Polarized distribution and activation of Wnt-Fz/PCP components triggers spatially confined changes in the cytoskeletal architecture of epithelial cells leading to their morphological recognizable polarization.
source: This polarized distribution and activation of Wnt-Fz/PCP components is thought to trigger spatially confined changes in the cytoskeletal architecture of epithelial cells leading to their morphological recognizable polarization (Strutt and Warrington, 2008; Ségalen et al., 2010; Strutt et al., 2011; Butler and Wallingford, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and includes speculative language ('is thought to').

claim: Much less is known about how Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling controls mesenchymal cell polarization and movement.
source: In contrast, much less is known about how Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling controls mesenchymal cell polarization and movement (Shindo and Wallingford, 2014).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling components with a known function in epithelial PCP are required for proper cell polarization and intercalation in mesenchymal cells.
source: Previous studies on non-canonical Wnt signaling in mesenchymal cells have demonstrated that Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling components with a known function in epithelial PCP are required for proper cell polarization and intercalation (Gray et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Prickle (Pk) and Dishevelled (Dsh) localize preferentially to the anterior or posterior site of mesenchymal cells, respectively.
source: Moreover, the Wnt-Fz/PCP core components Prickle (Pk) and Dishevelled (Dsh) have been shown to localize preferentially to the anterior or posterior site of mesenchymal cells, respectively, pointing to the possibility that localized activity of these components triggers mesenchymal cell polarization (Ciruna et al., 2006; Yin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Graded Wnt11 signals can direct myoblast cell elongation.
source: Likewise, studies on the role of non-canonical Wnt signaling in mesenchymal myoblast cells provided evidence for the capacity of graded Wnt11 signals in directing myoblast cell elongation (Gros et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Uniform overexpression of non-canonical Wnt signaling ligands can rescue defective mesenchymal cell polarization in Wnt-Fz/PCP mutant embryos.
source: In contrast, the observation that uniform overexpression of non-canonical Wnt signaling ligands can rescue defective mesenchymal cell polarization in Wnt-Fz/PCP mutant embryos (Heisenberg et al., 2000) points to a permissive function of Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling in this process (Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Direct evidence for non-canonical Wnt signaling exerting either instructive or permissive functions in mesenchymal cell polarization and intercalation is still lacking.
source: While these overexpression and localization studies suggest both a permissive and instructive role for Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling in mesenchymal cell polarization and intercalation, direct evidence for non-canonical Wnt signaling exerting either of these functions is still lacking.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: In MZfz7a/b double mutants, the ppl is elongated and placed closer to the anterior end of the notochord at the end of gastrulation.
source: Our analysis showed that in MZfz7a/b double mutants, beside the previously reported dorsal convergence defects (Quesada-Hernández et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 1), the ppl was elongated and placed closer to the anterior end of the notochord at the end of gastrulation (bud stage, 10 hrs post-fertilization, hpf) (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Wild type ppl progenitors migrate with a velocity of 2–3 μm/min towards the animal pole.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Smutny et al., 2017), we found that wt ppl progenitors migrated with a velocity of 2–3 μm/min towards the animal pole, and that at late gastrulation (90% epiboly) this movement was highly correlated with the movement of overlying ectoderm progenitors (Figure 1G&H, Video 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G&H and Video 1, and is consistent with prior work.

claim: At late gastrulation (90% epiboly), wild type ppl progenitor movement is highly correlated with the movement of overlying ectoderm progenitors.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Smutny et al., 2017), we found that wt ppl progenitors migrated with a velocity of 2–3 μm/min towards the animal pole, and that at late gastrulation (90% epiboly) this movement was highly correlated with the movement of overlying ectoderm progenitors (Figure 1G&H, Video 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ppl progenitors in MZfz7a/b mutant embryos slow down their animal pole directed movement during gastrulation and eventually move backwards towards the vegetal pole from mid-gastrulation on.
source: In comparison, ppl progenitors in MZfz7a/b mutant embryos slowed down their animal pole directed movement during gastrulation, and eventually even moved backwards towards the vegetal pole from mid-gastrulation on (Figure 1F&H, Video 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and velocity data shown in Figure 1F&H and Video 1.

claim: Movement coordination between ppl and ectoderm progenitors remains unchanged in MZfz7a/b mutant embryos.
source: Interestingly, movement coordination between ppl and ectoderm progenitors remained unchanged in MZfz7a/b mutant embryos (Figure 1G, Figure 1—source data 1), arguing against a previously suggested function of Fz7 in controlling the interaction between ppl and overlying ectoderm (Winklbauer et al., 2001; Montero et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1G and argues against prior hypotheses.

claim: When wild type cells are transplanted into the ppl of MZfz7a/b mutant embryos, these cells typically move to the leading edge of the ppl and show lower movement correlation with their neighboring host cells compared to transplanted mutant cells in mutant embryos.
source: When wt cells were transplanted into the ppl of MZfz7a/b mutant embryos, these cells typically moved to the leading edge of the ppl and showed lower movement correlation with their neighboring host cells when compared to transplanted mutant cells in mutant embryos (Figure 2A&D, Video 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 2A&D and Video 2.

claim: Mutant ppl progenitors transplanted into the ppl of wild type embryos typically end up closer to the posterior end of the ppl and show reduced movement correlation with their wild type neighboring cells compared to transplanted wild type cells in wild type embryos.
source: Conversely, mutant ppl progenitors transplanted into the ppl of wt embryos typically ended up closer to the posterior end of the ppl and showed reduced movement correlation with their wt neighboring cells when compared to transplanted wt cells in wt embryos (Figure 2A&C, Video 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 2A&C and Video 2.

claim: Fz7 functions cell-autonomously in ppl progenitors by determining their ability for undergoing directed migration.
source: Together, these transplantation experiments suggest that Fz7 functions cell-autonomously in ppl progenitors by determining their ability for undergoing directed migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the transplantation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: After 4 hrs in culture, wild type ppl progenitors at the margin of clusters show pronounced substrate spreading and form multiple protrusions resembling lamellipodia (54% of cells on the margin of clusters).
source: We found that after 4 hrs in culture wt progenitors at the margin of these clusters showed pronounced substrate spreading and formed multiple protrusions, resembling lamellipodia (54% of cells on the margin of clusters; Figure 3A&B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture experiments shown in Figure 3A&B.

claim: Ppl progenitors from MZfz7a/b mutant embryos form significantly less lamellipodia-like protrusions (27% of marginal cells) compared to wild type.
source: Ppl progenitors from MZfz7a/b mutant embryos, in contrast, formed significantly less lamellipodia-like protrusions (27% of marginal cells; Figure 3A&B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture experiments shown in Figure 3A&B.

claim: Fz7 is required for the formation of lamellipodia in ppl progenitors during substrate spreading.
source: This suggests that Fz7 is required for the formation of lamellipodia in ppl progenitors during substrate spreading.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro protrusion formation data.

claim: Ppl cells form significantly less protrusions resembling lamellipodia or pseudopodia in MZfz7a/b mutants (0.14 ± 0.059 protrusions/cell/minute) compared to wild type embryos (0.33 ± 0.075 protrusions/cell/minute).
source: Consistent with our in vitro observations, ppl cells formed significantly less protrusions resembling lamellipodia or pseudopodia in MZfz7a/b mutants (0.14 ± 0.059 protrusions/cell/minute) compared to wt embryos (0.33 ± 0.075 protrusions/cell/minute), while the number of blebs increased and of protrusions resembling filopodia remained largely unchanged (Figure 3C–F, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C-F and Video 3.

claim: The number of blebs increases in MZfz7a/b mutants compared to wild type embryos.
source: Consistent with our in vitro observations, ppl cells formed significantly less protrusions resembling lamellipodia or pseudopodia in MZfz7a/b mutants (0.14 ± 0.059 protrusions/cell/minute) compared to wt embryos (0.33 ± 0.075 protrusions/cell/minute), while the number of blebs increased and of protrusions resembling filopodia remained largely unchanged (Figure 3C–F, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C-F and Video 3.

claim: The number of protrusions resembling filopodia remains largely unchanged in MZfz7a/b mutants compared to wild type embryos.
source: Consistent with our in vitro observations, ppl cells formed significantly less protrusions resembling lamellipodia or pseudopodia in MZfz7a/b mutants (0.14 ± 0.059 protrusions/cell/minute) compared to wt embryos (0.33 ± 0.075 protrusions/cell/minute), while the number of blebs increased and of protrusions resembling filopodia remained largely unchanged (Figure 3C–F, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C-F and Video 3.

claim: The preferential orientation of different protrusion types in the direction of ppl progenitor cell migration towards the animal pole is indistinguishable between MZfz7a/b and wild type embryos.
source: Importantly, the preferential orientation of these different protrusion types in the direction of ppl progenitor cell migration towards the animal pole was indistinguishable between MZfz7a/b and wt embryos (Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by orientation analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Fz7 is required for the type but not orientation of protrusions formed in leading edge ppl cells.
source: Together, this suggests that Fz7 is required for the type but not orientation of protrusions formed in leading edge ppl cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the protrusion type and orientation data.

claim: Opto-Fz7 was designed based on zebrafish Fz7 and bovine Rhodopsin.
source: Opto-Fz7 was designed based on zebrafish Fz7 (NCBI NM_131139.1) and bovine Rhodopsin (NCBI NM_001014890.2).
evidence: This describes the design of the Opto-Fz7 construct.

claim: The intracellular domains of rhodopsin were substituted with the corresponding domains of fz7 to create Opto-Fz7.
source: Following this rationale, we substituted the intracellular domains of the light-sensitive receptor rhodopsin with the corresponding domains of fz7 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the protein engineering approach shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The inactive and active state conformations of Rhodopsin and Smoothened can be superimposed revealing a conserved arrangement of the TM helices.
source: We found that the inactive and active state conformations of Rhodopsin and Smoothened (Smo), a surrogate receptor for Fz7 and the sole Class F GPCR for which inactive and active state structures are available, can be superimposed revealing a conserved arrangement of the TM helices (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; RMSD 2.8 and 2.6 Å for the inactive and active states, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rhodopsin and Smoothened have similar numbers of inter-helical contacts that stabilize these receptors in both inactive and active receptor states.
source: In addition, analysis of non-covalent contact networks (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016; Kayikci et al., 2018) revealed similar numbers of inter-helical contacts that stabilize these receptors again in both receptor states (inactive state: 223 and 217 contacts for Rhodopsin and Smo; active state: 197 and 173 contacts for Rhodopsin and Smo).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis of protein structures.

claim: The Opto-Fz7 receptor variant containing the ICL3 and C-terminal intracellular domains of Fz7 shows clear and uniform localization at the plasma membrane of all progenitor cell types analyzed within the gastrulating embryo at 70% epiboly stage.
source: Following ectopic expression by mRNA injection at the one-cell stage, the second receptor variant containing the ICL3 and C-terminal intracellular domains of Fz7 showed clear and uniform localization at the plasma membrane of all progenitor cell types analyzed within the gastrulating embryo at 70% epiboly stage, including ppl, epiblast, nc and paraxial mesendoderm cells (7 hpf; Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Opto-Fz7 re-localizes from the plasma membrane to intracellular vesicles upon light exposure.
source: We found Opto-Fz7 to re-localize from the plasma membrane to intracellular vesicles upon light exposure (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that Opto-Fz7 signaling is activated by light.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Zebrafish Dvl2-GFP co-localizes with Opto-Fz7-mCherry at the plasma membrane.
source: We found that zebrafish Dvl2-GFP co-localized with Opto-Fz7-mCherry at the plasma membrane, and that Dvl, much like Opto-Fz7, was endocytosed upon light activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A&B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A&B.

claim: Dvl is endocytosed upon light activation of Opto-Fz7.
source: We found that zebrafish Dvl2-GFP co-localized with Opto-Fz7-mCherry at the plasma membrane, and that Dvl, much like Opto-Fz7, was endocytosed upon light activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A&B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A&B.

claim: No recognizable changes in nuclear β-catenin localization are detected upon light activation of Opto-Fz7 in embryos at 5.5 hpf.
source: In contrast, we detected no recognizable changes in nuclear β-catenin localization upon light activation of Opto-Fz7 in embryos at 5.5 hpf, while uniform overexpression of the canonical Wnt ligand Wnt8 elicited nuclear accumulation of β-catenin throughout the embryo (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C–F, Figure 4 – source data; Brunet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C-F.

claim: Uniform overexpression of the canonical Wnt ligand Wnt8 elicits nuclear accumulation of β-catenin throughout the embryo.
source: In contrast, we detected no recognizable changes in nuclear β-catenin localization upon light activation of Opto-Fz7 in embryos at 5.5 hpf, while uniform overexpression of the canonical Wnt ligand Wnt8 elicited nuclear accumulation of β-catenin throughout the embryo (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C–F, Figure 4 – source data; Brunet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C-F and a citation.

claim: Opto-Fz7 can be used for spatiotemporally controlled activation of non-canonical Fz7 signaling within the ppl.
source: Together, these findings indicate that Opto-Fz7 can be used for spatiotemporally controlled activation of non-canonical Fz7 signaling within the ppl.
evidence: This is inferred from the characterization experiments showing Dvl recruitment and lack of β-catenin nuclear accumulation.

claim: Local activation of Opto-Fz7 in cultured clusters of MZfz7a/b mutant ppl progenitor cells triggers movement of the entire cell cluster in the direction of the activated region within the cluster.
source: We found that local activation of Opto-Fz7 in these clusters triggered movement of the entire cell cluster in the direction of the activated region within the cluster (Figure 4D&E, Video 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4D&E and Video 4.

claim: Cluster movement upon local Opto-Fz7 activation is accompanied by increased protrusion formation at the light-exposed side of the explant.
source: This cluster movement was accompanied by increased protrusion formation at the light-exposed side of the explant (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A&B, Figure 4 – source data, Video 4), suggesting that localized stimulation of cell motility by unilateral Opto-Fz7 activation triggers this movement.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A&B and Video 4.

claim: When Fz7 is activated in one half of the ppl in vivo, the ppl motion is biased to the direction of the activated side.
source: Strikingly, we found that the ppl motion was biased to the direction of the activated side (Figure 4F&G, Figure 4—figure supplement 5E&F, Figure 4 – source data, Video 5), an effect that could be effectively reverted by switching the activation of Fz7 to the initially non-activated side of the ppl (Figure 4G, Figure 4 – source data, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4F&G and Video 5.

claim: The redirection of ppl motion by localized Fz7 activation can be effectively reverted by switching the activation of Fz7 to the initially non-activated side of the ppl.
source: Strikingly, we found that the ppl motion was biased to the direction of the activated side (Figure 4F&G, Figure 4—figure supplement 5E&F, Figure 4 – source data, Video 5), an effect that could be effectively reverted by switching the activation of Fz7 to the initially non-activated side of the ppl (Figure 4G, Figure 4 – source data, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4G and Video 5.

claim: The activated side of the ppl shows a higher number of lamellipodia-like protrusions at the leading edge compared to the non-activated side.
source: Furthermore, comparing protrusion formation at the leading edge of the activated versus non-activated side of the ppl showed a higher number of lamellipodia-like protrusions at the activated side (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C&D, Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that Fz7 redirects ppl migration by triggering protrusion formation locally within the ppl.
evidence: This is supported by protrusion quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5C&D.

claim: Control MZfz7a/b mutant embryos expressing Rhodopsin instead of Opto-Fz7 do not show any redirection of ppl cell migration upon half-sided light stimulation.
source: In contrast, control MZfz7a/b mutant embryos expressing Rhodopsin instead of Opto-Fz7 did not show any redirection of ppl cell migration upon half-sided light stimulation (Figure 4F&G, Figure 4—figure supplement 5E&F, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 4F&G.

claim: Locally restricted activation of Fz7 has the capability of redirecting ppl cell migration.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that locally restricted activation of Fz7 has the capability of redirecting ppl cell migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the localized optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Reduced protrusion formation at the margin of small clusters of MZfz7a/b mutant ppl progenitors in culture is fully rescued by uniform activation of Fz7 signaling.
source: Protrusion formation was fully rescued in cultured clusters of MZfz7a/b mutant ppl progenitors upon uniform light activation of Opto-Fz7 in these cells (Figure 5A&B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro rescue experiments shown in Figure 5A&B.

claim: Uniform over-activation of Fz7 signaling in wild type ppl cell clusters by uniform light activation of Opto-Fz7 leads to reduced protrusion formation.
source: Moreover, uniform over-activation of Fz7signaling in wt ppl cell clusters by uniform light activation of Opto-Fz7 led to reduced protrusion formation (Figure 5A&B, Figure 5—source data 1), consistent with previous observations that over-activation of Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling mimics the loss-of-function phenotype (Heisenberg et al., 2000; Kilian et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experiments shown in Figure 5A&B and is consistent with prior observations.

claim: Uniform activation of Fz7 signaling in MZfz7a/b mutant embryos expressing Opto-Fz7 fully rescues ppl movement as judged by ppl shape and distance to the anterior tip of the notochord.
source: Strikingly, we found that uniform activation of Fz7 signaling in MZfz7a/b mutant embryos expressing Opto-Fz7 fully rescued ppl movement as judged by ppl shape and distance to the anterior tip of the notochord (Figure 5C–E, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo rescue experiments shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Uniform activation of Fz7 in ppl cells can fully rescue their cell-autonomous migration and protrusion formation defects when transplanted into the ppl of a wild type embryo.
source: Likewise, we found that uniform activation of Fz7 in ppl cells could fully rescue their cell-autonomous migration and protrusion formation defects when transplanted into the ppl of a wt embryo (Figure 5F–I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Video 6 and 7, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by transplantation rescue experiments shown in Figure 5F-I and Videos 6 and 7.

claim: No rescue activity is detected in control conditions (absence of light, Rhodopsin overexpression together with 9-cis-retinal injection, and 9-cis-retinal injection alone).
source: In contrast, no such rescue activity was detected in control conditions (absence of light, Rhodopsin overexpression together with 9-cis-retinal injection, and 9-cis-retinal injection alone; Figure 5C–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 5C-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fz7 signaling has a permissive function in ppl cell protrusion formation and directed migration during gastrulation.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Fz7 signaling has a permissive function in ppl cell protrusion formation and directed migration during gastrulation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the uniform activation rescue experiments.

claim: Uniform activation of Fz7 could not rescue the convergence phenotypes of the notochord and the paraxial mesoderm.
source: Also, uniform activation of Fz7 could not rescue the convergence phenotypes of the notochord and the paraxial mesoderm (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that the mode of Fz7 function might be context-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fz7 signaling is required for the formation of actin-rich lamellipodia-like protrusions in ppl cells.
source: Our finding that Fz7 signaling is required for the formation of actin-rich lamellipodia-like protrusions in ppl cells, suggests that Fz7 enables directed ppl cell migration by promoting protrusion formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the protrusion formation data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: There is no evidence for a clearly recognizable polarized subcellular distribution of Fz7 or any other Wnt-Fz/PCP components in ppl cells.
source: In contrast, we found no evidence for a clearly recognizable polarized subcellular distribution of Fz7 or any other Wnt-Fz/PCP components in ppl cells (Figure 4B, Figure 5—figure supplement 4, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that endogenous Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling might be uniform rather than polarized in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Ppl cells do not endogenously express Wnt11.
source: Notably, while our data suggest that Wnt11/Fz7 signaling is required for directed ppl cell migration, ppl cells do not endogenously express Wnt11.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about gene expression.

claim: Wnt11 is expressed in the anterior paraxial mesendoderm close to the ppl.
source: However, Wnt11 is expressed in the anterior paraxial mesendoderm close to the ppl (Heisenberg et al., 2000; Kilian et al., 2003), pointing to the possibility that Wnt11 secreted by the anterior paraxial mesendoderm acts on adjacent ppl cells, thereby promoting protrusion formation and directed migration of these cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Signaling through the Wnt receptor Fz7, although being required for mesenchymal cell polarization and directed migration, has no direct function in polarizing those cells.
source: Our findings show that signaling through the Wnt receptor Fz7, although being required for mesenchymal cell polarization and directed migration, has no direct function in polarizing those cells; it rather promotes protrusion formation, allowing the cells to undergo directed migration.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from all the experimental data.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling can have very different functions depending on the specific cellular context in which it acts.
source: This suggests that non-canonical Wnt-Fz/PCP signaling can have very different functions depending on the specific cellular context in which it acts.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the findings of the study.
